trap: Mostly guessable, but 'talk about X' is usually X no hanashi (o suru), shorter than X ni tsuite hanasu.
Learners say suki for 'I love it!' about something new; natives say ki ni itta, and iru here conjugates godan (itta), not like iru 'be' (ita).
'Have time' takes aru/nai, not motsu.
Not junbi desu or redi: 'Are you ready?' is junbi dekita?, where ready means the preparation has come into being.
English 'disturb/bother' has no matching verb: it is jama (o) suru, and entering someone's home is the set phrase ojama shimasu.
Not benri for people and advice: 'useful' or 'helpful' is yaku ni tatsu. Benri means convenient.
Not uso o hanasu or uso o suru: lies take tsuku (uso tsuite nai yo).
Not hanasu hitsuyou ga aru: 'I need to talk to you' is chotto hanashi ga aru n da kedo.
Not shitsumon o kiku: 'ask a question' is shitsumon (o) suru, and kiku alone means 'ask' without the noun.
Not jikan o toru: the time a task takes is kakaru (jikan o toru means setting time aside).
Not itaku naru or kizutsuku: an injury is 'done', kega o suru, even by accident (kega shita?).
'Have time' uses aru, not motsu.
Not yume o motsu (that's a life ambition): dreaming in your sleep is yume o miru, 'seeing' a dream.
Not ki o tsukeru: caring for a pet, child or plant is sewa o suru (inu no sewa).
'Interested' is an adjective in English; Japanese says kyoumi ga aru/nai.
English 'take care of' gives no clue: you 'see to the bother' with mendou o miru. Keep it apart from mendokusai (what a hassle).
'Lucky' is an adjective in English, but Japanese says un ga ii (your luck is good), or rakkii. Unlucky is un ga warui.

english: make sense; get what something means
trap: There's no 'make sense' verb: 'that makes no sense' is imi ga wakaranai (imi wakannai), 'the meaning can't be grasped'.
No 'hungry' adjective: the stomach empties, onaka suita, past tense for the feeling now.
Getting out of bed is okiru; me o samasu is coming awake.
Not tatakau, which means battle: a fight or argument between people is kenka suru (kare to kenka shita, with to).
'Interested' is not an adjective: X ni kyoumi ga aru. Learners say omoshiroi desu, which means 'it's interesting/funny'.
English 'notice' has no 'mind' word, so learners say miru or wakaru; and it is ki GA TSUKU, not ki o tsukeru (be careful).

english: feel good, be in a good mood
trap: 'Feel good' is not kanjiru; mood is kibun ga ii, physical comfort kimochi ii.
No single verb for 'ruin'; say dainashi ni suru/naru.

english: get in a car, ride in a car
trap: Takes ni, not o; 'get in' is noru, not hairu.

english: be pleasant, nice (a person or place)
trap: For a pleasant manner or vibe, not yasashii: kanji ga ii, as in kanji no ii hito / kanji warui.
Not kodomo o motte iru or kodomo ga aru: people you 'have' take ga iru (kodomo iru? kyoudai iru? kareshi iru?).
'I know how you feel' is sono kimochi wakaru, not shitteru: shiru is for knowing facts.
Not kao o tsukuru: wearing an expression is kao o suru, as in hen na kao shiteru or sonna kao shinaide.
Not nioi o kagu or nioi da: 'it smells good' is ii nioi ga suru, with suru.
kiru only covers tops and whole-body clothes (shirt, coat, dress, kimono). English 'wear' also covers shoes, trousers, hats and glasses, which each take a different verb.
Not kotaeru: picking up the phone is denwa ni deru ('come out to the phone'); kotaeru answers a question.
'Call' meaning summon is yobu; denwa suru is only phoning.
A voice you just happen to hear is koe ga kikoeru.

english: get in touch, stay in contact
trap: Not renraku o morau or tamotsu: making or keeping contact is toru (mada renraku totteru? / renraku ga torenai).
'Have a question' is aru, not motsu.
Takes ni, not o.
Not furuku naru (that's for things): people 'take years', toshi o toru (toshi totta naa).
Eyes take tojiru (or tsuburu), not shimeru.
The place you leave takes o: ie o deru.
'Put back' is moto ni modosu, not oku.
Not only okiru: waking from sleep is me ga sameru ('eyes wake'); okiru is getting up.
'Be helpful' is tasuke ni naru, not tetsudau.

english: wait and see, keep an eye on it
trap: Not matsu: 'let's wait and see' is yousu o miru ('watch how things look').
'Leave me alone' is hitori ni shite, not oite iku.
No single everyday verb for 'breathe'; say iki o suru.
Not tanoshii or ii kanji for a bath, breeze or massage: physical pleasantness is kimochi ii.
Not sumaato (that means slim and stylish): 'smart' is atama ga ii. Kashikoi exists but is less everyday.
Not kokoro o kaeru: changing your mind is ki ga kawaru, with ki as the subject (ki ga kawattara itte).

english: wrap up, call it a day
trap: Ending a session is owari ni suru; owaru alone is intransitive.
'Talented' is an adjective; Japanese says sainou ga aru.
Not yobu or iu: phoning someone is denwa o kakeru (or simply denwa suru); yobu is summon, iu is call something a name.
Means physically sick or queasy, not 'grumpy' (that is kigen ga warui); kimochi warui is the casual twin.
'See a doctor' is byouin ni iku (go to the clinic), not isha ni au; byouin covers any clinic.
Not doa ga akeru: when it opens by itself or is open, use aku (doa aiteru yo); akeru needs someone to do it.
English 'lie down' has no Japanese verb a learner could guess: it's 'become sideways', yoko ni naru. It has nothing to do with the 'lie' of uso o tsuku.
Not geemu o asobu: asobu takes no game object, so a game is done with suru or yaru (geemu yatteta).

english: light the stove or a fire; light a cigarette
trap: English 'light' has no obvious verb; it is tsukeru, the same verb as for lights, and hi o tsukete sounds like ki o tsukete (be careful).
'Gross/creepy' and 'I feel queasy' are both kimochi warui; learners reach for kirai or byouki.
There is no verb for 'complain': you 'say complaints', as in monku iwanaide (guchi o iu = grumble, vent).
Not yakusoku o motsu or tamotsu: keeping a promise is mamoru, 'protect' (jikan o mamoru = be on time).
'I had a scary experience' is kowai omoi o shita, not kowai keiken o motta: the feeling is the object of suru.
No 'thirsty' adjective: the throat dries, nodo kawaita, past tense for the feeling now.
English makes the hearer the subject; Japanese makes the voice the subject with ga kikoeru, not o kiku.
Not kuruma o paaku suru: parking is just 'stopping' the car, tomeru (chuusha suru is the word on signs). Not yameru, which means quitting.
English 'have problems' leads to motsu; Japanese says kakaeru or mondai ga aru.

english: have no time, money or room to spare
trap: There's no verb for 'afford': 'I can't afford it' and 'I'm swamped' are both yoyuu ga nai (no margin).
English 'hit' leads to tataku or naguru; bumping your own head is utsu.
English 'have' leads to motsu; experience takes ga aru.
Japanese has no verb for 'look forward': you 'make it a pleasure', as in tanoshimi ni shiteru (ne).
English 'grow up' leads to sodatsu; becoming an adult is otona ni naru.
Not kanjiru: 'I feel sick' has no feel verb; the condition is bad, guai ga warui.
English 'lock' gives no verb: you kakeru the key, and 'it's locked' is kagi ga kakatteru (kagi o shimeru is also heard).
Not kanjiru for 'it feels like...': the everyday form is ~ kanji ga suru (or ~ tte kanji).

english: go back to how it was

trap: English 'smoke' is one verb; Japanese 'inhales' tobacco (tabako o suu). kemuri (smoke) is no help.
Not shawaa o toru: you abiru (pour over yourself) a shower.
Not tomodachi o tsukuru: 'make friends with X' is X to tomodachi ni naru, while tomodachi ga dekiru means gaining friends in general.
English 'call me' leads to yobu (summon); a phone call is denwa (o) kureru or denwa shite.
English 'be interested' is an adjective; Japanese uses the noun kyoumi with motsu or ga aru, and ni for the topic.
English 'affect' is one verb; Japanese uses the noun eikyou with ataeru (or ukeru for being affected).
English 'oneself' leads to jibun o mamoru; the set uses mi.
There is no verb for this: 'we get along' is naka ga ii (the relationship is good). This naka is not naka 'inside'.
There is no verb for 'thank': you 'say thanks' with orei o iu (orei also means a thank-you gift).
Not just renraku dekinai: 'I can't reach him' is renraku ga torenai (or renraku ga tsukanai).
English 'I didn't mean it' leads to imi; Japanese says warugi wa nakatta.

english: be good at one's job, be capable
trap: Not shigoto ga jouzu: being good at your job is dekiru, usually shigoto ga dekiru hito.
Not ame ga ochiru, and English 'it rains' has no Japanese verb of its own: rain and snow fall with furu.
English 'get caught in the rain' points to tsukamaru. Japanese uses the suffering passive of furu with ni: ame ni furareta.
Not shigoto o deru or a 'get off' verb: you say the work itself ends, shigoto ga owaru (shigoto owatta? nanji ni owaru?).
Not ki o tsukeru (be careful): tsukau means fussing over others, as in ki o tsukawanaide (don't go to any trouble).
Not jikan o tsukau or sugosu: putting time into something is kakeru (jikan kakete tsukutta), the transitive of kakaru.
Not tsukau, which treats time as a resource you use up. Spending time with people, or spending a weekend, is sugosu (shuumatsu dou sugoshita?).
Particle is ni, not o; noru covers every vehicle.
English 'answer' leads to kotae, which is an answer to a question; replying to a person, message or call is henji (o) suru.
English 'leave' leads to saru or hanareru; leaving a place is o deru.
Not meiwaku o suru or tsukuru: you 'hang' trouble on people with kakeru (meiwaku kakete gomen).

english: blame (someone else), pin it on someone
trap: Not semeru, which means 'criticise, attack'. To pin the blame on someone is X no sei ni suru.
Not joudan o tsukuru or suru: a joke is 'said', and joudan da yo means just kidding.
Not byouki o toru or byouki ga dekiru: illness is something you 'become' (ni naru).
Not kusuri o toru: medicine is 'drunk', kusuri o nomu, even pills.
Not 'kare wa takai' or 'nagai': height is se ga takai, and takai alone sounds like 'expensive'.

english: hear a sound, there's a noise
trap: Not oto o kiku: you don't 'hear a noise', the noise 'does' it: nanka oto ga shita.
Not himitsu o motsu or tamotsu. You keep a secret with mamoru (protect), the same verb as yakusoku o mamoru.
English 'wear' is one verb; Japanese splits it: kiru for suits and tops, haku for trousers and shoes.
English 'it smells good' sends learners looking for a verb; Japanese says ii nioi (ga suru).
Not kakeru (hang): denwa o kakeru makes the call; ending it is kiru ('cut').

english: make a hole; get (one's ears) pierced
trap: Not ana o tsukuru. Making a hole is akeru, and getting your ears pierced is piasu (no ana) o akeru.
English 'in the sky' leads to de; moving through the sky takes o.
Not michi o nakusu or michi o ushinau: getting lost is michi ni mayou ('stray on the road'), or casually just mayotta.
Not onegai o kiku, which means agreeing to a favour: asking one opens with onegai ga aru n da kedo.
English 'follow' suggests tsuite iku; instructions take shitagau with ni.
English 'too late' leads to osoi; for something past saving it is teokure.

english: have something to do, have an errand
trap: Learners say suru koto ga aru or just isogashii. The standard vague excuse is chotto youji ga atte.
'I can't explain it' is setsumei ga tsukanai, not a form of setsumei suru.
Not benri: a time that suits someone is tsugou ga ii (benri is for tools and places). The opposite is tsugou ga warui, 'can't make it'.
'Tell me your name' uses oshieru, not iu.
'Get a chance' is kikai ga aru, not kikai o morau.
'I have a bad feeling about this' is iya na yokan ga suru, not warui kimochi ga aru, which sounds like nausea.
'Do my best' is zenryoku o tsukusu or ganbaru, never suru.
'Pack your things' is matomeru (gather up), not tsumeru.
'Get out of the car' is oriru (step down), not deru.
English 'close' suggests shimeru; mouths and eyes take tojiru.
'Make a mistake' is not tsukuru; say machigai o okasu or just machigaeru.
Not jikan ga tooru: time passing is tatsu (jikan tatsu no hayai ne), a different tatsu from 'stand'.

english: speak up; say it out loud
trap: English 'speak up' pushes toward hanasu. Japanese 'puts out the voice': motto koe dashite.
'I can't breathe' is iki ga dekinai; there is no single verb 'breathe'.
'I can't imagine' is usually souzou mo tsukanai, not souzou dekinai.
'Ask for opinions' uses kiku, not tanomu.
'I have a favor to ask' is tanomi ga aru, not a form of kiku.
'Take the bus' is noru with ni, not toru.
'Confident' is an adjective in English, but Japanese has confidence: jishin aru / jishin nai. (Jishin is also 'earthquake', as in jishin ga okiru.)
'Make trouble' is okosu (raise), not tsukuru.
Not e o hiku (that is sen o hiku, draw a line) or e o nuru (paint a wall): drawn or painted, a picture takes kaku.
Also means to apologize or ask humbly, not just a physical bow.
Not namae o ageru: you 'attach' a name (namae o tsukeru).

english: be worthwhile, do you good (advice, a book, an experience)
trap: Not yaku ni tatsu for advice or experiences: a tool is yaku ni tatsu, but something that does you good is tame ni naru.
'Make way' is akeru (clear), not tsukuru.
'This medicine works' is kouka ga aru or kiku, not hataraku.
'Live a happy life' is jinsei o okuru (send), not ikiru with jinsei.
'Can you hear me?' is kikoeru?, not kiku: kiku is deliberate listening, and the thing heard takes ga.
Not keikaku o tsukuru: plans are tateru, 'stand up'. yotei o tateru works the same way.
'I don't remember that' is often kioku ga nai, not only oboete inai.
'Look around' needs mawari (surroundings) as the object; there is no 'around' particle.
'I have no money' is okane ga nai, not motte inai.
yakusoku isn't only 'promise': it means any arrangement to meet, so kyou wa yakusoku ga aru = I'm meeting someone today.
'Take responsibility' is sekinin o motsu or toru, not ukeru.
'Leave a message' is nokosu, not deru or saru.
'Take someone' is tsurete iku; motte iku is only for things.
English 'go up and talk to' leads to hanasu; approaching someone is koe o kakeru (koe o dasu just means make a sound).
'Bleed' is one verb in English; Japanese says blood comes out, chi ga deru (chi deteru yo).
'I'm not sure I can' is jishin ga nai, not wakaranai.
'I have no experience' is keiken ga nai, not motte inai.
Not yotei o motsu: having plans is aru (yotei aru kara = I've got plans).

english: be off, not feel right; (a machine) act up
trap: Not just genki ja nai: choushi ga warui covers being off form, a bad stomach, or a phone or PC that's acting up.
'I'm sorry for your loss' is okuyami moushiagemasu, not sumimasen.
Not kekka o morau: results 'come out' (kekka ga deru). Getting good results yourself is kekka o dasu.
Are you hurt? is kega wa nai?, not itai desu ka.
Get some fresh air is soto no kuuki o suu; suu (inhale) does the work of 'breathe'.
Give me your number is bangou oshiete (teach/tell), not ageru or kudasai.
No adjective for 'confident'; say jishin o motsu or jishin ga aru.
There is no English equivalent: thanks for someone's help is osewa ni narimashita (you 'became' the one cared for), not sewa o shite kurete arigatou.
There's no verb for 'cheer up': you say genki dashite ('put out your energy').
'Take responsibility' is sekinin o toru; ou means carry it on your back.

english: step away (from one's desk or the table)
trap: Not seki o deru. Stepping away for a moment is hazusu ('remove'), as in the phone line tadaima seki o hazushite orimasu.
'Panic' is a verb in English, so learners say panikku suru; natives say panikku ni naru.
No 'look' verb: 'looks familiar' is mioboe ga aru (have a memory of seeing).
'Sit on' takes ni, not ue ni or de.

english: be shocked, be hurt (by news, a remark)
trap: Not shokku suru: you receive a shock, so shokku uketa. Shokku datta is the other natural way.
'Smell this!' is kaide mite: actively smelling is kagu, not nioi o suru or kiku.
'Have a party' is suru (or hiraku), not motsu.
'Get lost' is maigo ni naru (become a lost child), even for adults.
'Rely on' is not shinrai suru (trust); it is tayori ni suru.
Not kaze o toru or tsukamu: you 'pull' a cold, kaze o hiku (kaze hiichatta).
The pairing itself is guessable; the risk is transitivity, mado o akeru (you do it) vs mado ga aiteru (it's open).
'Have a heart attack' uses okosu (set off), not motsu.
English passive leads to eikyou sareru; natives say eikyou o ukeru (receive influence).
Not fuku o toru: every garment comes off with nugu, whichever verb put it on.
Not kakkou o kiru: 'dressed like that' is sonna kakkou shite. Kakkou means outfit or look.
'Take an interest' uses motsu (hold), not toru.
English 'wave' is one verb; Japanese shakes the hand, te o furu.

english: have a complaint, got a problem
trap: 'Complain' is monku o iu; nanka monku aru? is 'got a problem?'
Not kirei na tenki or yasashii tenki for 'a beautiful/nice day': good weather is just ii, and bad weather is warui.
Not sumaho o kesu: devices are powered off with dengen o kiru ('cut the power'). Kesu is for lights and TVs.
'Wear' splits by body part: kiru for dresses and tops, haku for skirts and trousers.
'Any idea where it went?' is kokoroatari aru?, not aidia.
English 'it's locked' has no noun in it, so learners can't guess kagi ga kakatteru. It's the intransitive partner of kagi o kakeru.
There is no phrasal verb for 'make up': it is nakanaori suru ('mending the relationship'), never tsukuru.
'Do your best' is not besuto o suru; it is besuto o tsukusu (or ganbaru).
Not te o motsu: holding hands is 'linking' them with tsunagu, the same verb as netto ni tsunagu.
'Are you serious?' is honki de itteru?, not majime (earnest by nature).
Not raido o ageru: giving a lift uses noseru ('put on board'), the transitive of noru. To ask for one: nosete kureru?
Not me o shimeru: shimeru is for doors and windows. Eyes take tsuburu (casual) or tojiru (neutral).
Not oto o tsukuru: 'make a noise' is oto o tateru ('raise' a sound).
Not hazukashii ni naru: making a fool of yourself is haji o kaku, with the same kaku as ase o kaku and ibiki o kaku.

english: have time or money to spare; be relaxed about it
trap: English 'can afford' or 'have time to spare' has no single verb here; Japanese uses yoyuu ga aru / nai for time, money and calm.
'Raise your voice' tempts ageru; Japanese puts out (dasu) a big voice.
'Lead/live a life' uses okuru (send), not michibiku.

english: drive (someone), offer to take the car
trap: Not unten suru when offering a lift: 'I'll drive' is kuruma dasu yo ('take the car out').

english: be expecting, have a baby on the way
trap: Not kodomo o motsu: 'we're having a baby' is kodomo ga dekita. Kodomo ga iru means you already have children.
'Have courage' is aru/nai, not motsu.
'Throw/have a party': Japanese opens (hiraku) it.
'Lose' is ushinau here, not nakusu.
'Get treatment' tempts morau; Japanese receives it with ukeru.
'Take action' is not toru; Japanese raises (okosu) it.

english: work up the courage, be brave
trap: Not yuuki o motsu or mitsukeru: you 'put out' courage, yuuki o dasu (yuuki dashite itta), as in genki o dasu.
Not yakusoku o kowasu: breaking a promise is yaburu, 'tear'.
Not kutsu o kiru: anything on the feet or legs takes haku.
'I'm not free/busy' maps to tsugou ga warui, not hima ja nai.
Sounds like naru 'become', but this is 鳴る 'ring': keitai natteru yo = 'your phone's ringing'.
'Distracted/distracting' has no adjective in Japanese: ki ga chiru (urusakute ki ga chiru); learners only manage shuuchuu dekinai.

english: be reliable, dependable (someone you can count on)
trap: There is no plain adjective for 'reliable': a dependable person 'becomes a support', tayori ni naru. Tayori ni suru means 'rely on someone'.
'Have a meeting' is kaigi ga aru, not motsu.
'Have a baby' is umu (give birth), not motsu.
'Have a headache' is zutsuu ga suru, not motsu or aru.
'Wear' splits by body part: kiru for tops, haku for bottoms.
'Wear' a mask is tsukeru (or suru), not kiru.
'Make a mistake' is not tsukuru; okasu, or casually misu suru.
Toggles take on ni suru; tsukeru is for lights and TVs.
oboeru is memorise/keep in mind; recalling on the spot is omoidasu.
Sit takes ni (into the seat), not o.
'Fasten/buckle' is shimeru (tighten), not tsukeru.
'Morning comes' is asa ni naru (becomes), not kuru.
'Sweat' is a verb in English; Japanese 'scratches out' sweat: ase o kaku, not ase suru.
Not te ga yakeru or moeru: burning your skin is the noun yakedo + suru, like kega o suru.
'Turn around' is muku (face), not mawaru (spin).
Not boushi o kiru: anything pulled over the head (hat, cap, helmet, hood) takes kaburu.

english: have a baby (a child is born)
trap: Not kodomo o motsu or kodomo ga aru: 'we had a baby' is kodomo ga umareta (or akachan ga umareta), with the child as subject.
'Ask out' is sasou with ni, not kiku (ask a question).
Settings and toggles take ofu ni suru; kesu is for lights and TVs.
No single verb for 'be ruined'; it is dainashi ni naru (dainashi ni suru to ruin it).
Not jiko o shita or jiko o motta: being in an accident is jiko ni au, the same sound as meeting someone. A driver who causes one jiko o okosu.
There's no single verb for 'feed': you give the food (esa o yaru or ageru), with the same yaru as mizu o yaru.
With tabi the verb is deru (go out), not iku.
'Take pride' uses motsu (hold), not toru.
'I heard someone's voice' is koe ga shita (suru) when it just reaches you, not koe o kiita.
Not kibun ga warui, which means feeling sick: a bad mood is kigen ga warui. A good mood is kigen ga ii or gokigen.
English 'taste' is a verb; Japanese says the flavour 'does': ichigo no aji ga suru, not ichigo o ajiwau.
Not yume ga hontou ni naru: dreams are 'granted' (kanau).
'Get into trouble' is the passive makikomareru with ni, not hairu.
'Next to' is tonari; tsugi means next in order.
'Have tea' is nomu; motsu would mean holding it.
'In bed' takes de (place of action), not naka.
Dreams are seen (miru), not had (motsu).
'I feel well' is guai ga ii, not kanjiru.
'Wear' splits by body part; uniforms take kiru.
Rules are broken with yaburu (tear), not kowasu.
'Check email' is usually just miru.
Not takushii o kakeru: kakeru goes with denwa (the phone call), while the taxi you summon is yobu.
Intransitive shimaru (it closes) vs transitive shimeru (close it).
Screams are raised (ageru), not dasu.
Not eru, and usually not morau: 'I got a message' is meeru kita ('a message came').

english: get a haircut, cut one's hair
trap: Not kami o kitte morau or a 'haircut' noun: Japanese says kami kitta even when a hairdresser did the cutting.
'Put pressure' is kakeru, not oku.

english: be informative; learn a lot (from it)
trap: Not benkyou shita: 'that's really useful to know' is benkyou ni naru (benkyou ni narimashita), and nobody is studying.
Not koe ga takai, which means high-pitched, and not just urusai: a loud voice is ookii (big).
'Flush' has no Japanese verb of its own: you make the water flow, as in toire no mizu nagashite.
'Carry bags' is motsu; hakobu is moving them somewhere.
'Have a phone (on you)' is motte iru, not aru.
Not inu o motsu or inu ga aru: pets are 'kept' (kau, which sounds like 'buy'). You can also say inu ga iru.
'Make coffee' is ireru, not tsukuru.
Consciousness returns (modoru) on its own; there is no 'regain' verb.
Quoted words take to: noo to iu.
'Have plans' is yotei ga aru, not motsu.
Not kao ga aoi or kao ga shiroi: 'you look pale' is kaoiro ga warui (your complexion is bad).
'Break' suggests kowasu; rules and promises are yaburu (tear).
English says 'I start early'; Japanese makes the morning the subject.
English 'slow down' has no noun; Japanese drops (otosu) the speed.
'Save' suggests setsuyaku or tameru; effort is cut out with habuku.
No English verb matches: the day 'closes', hi ga kureru (casually kuraku naru). This kureru is unrelated to kureru 'give me'.
On the stove you 'put out the fire' (hi keshita?), not gasu o shimeru. Turning it on is hi o tsukeru.

english: hear from someone (they get in touch)
trap: Not X kara kiku, which means you heard some news from X. "Did he get in touch?" is renraku kita?
English 'I have no idea' tempts aidia ga nai or wakaranai; for 'no idea who or what it could be' Japanese uses kokoroatari ga nai.
Not a 'have' sentence: the head hurts, atama ga itai; zutsuu is the written word.
Keep it apart from shigoto o sagasu (look for one) and shigoto ga mitsukaru (one turns up): mitsukeru is the transitive 'find'.
'Start' suggests hajimeru; engines are kakeru.
'Miss' has no single verb; chances are nogasu, trains noriokureru.
English says 'I can't feel'; Japanese says there is no sensation.
Not ha o burashi suru or haku: teeth are migaku'd (polished).
The bridge takes o as the route crossed, not ni.
Not ofuro o toru: you 'enter' the bath, so it's ofuro ni hairu.
Not okane o sugosu: money is spent with tsukau, 'use'; sugosu is only for spending time.
English 'glad' tempts ureshii; relief that someone is safe is yokatta.
English 'have guests'; Japanese says the guests come.
'Make a fire' suggests tsukuru; fires are okosu (raise).
Not shujutsu o suru, which is what the surgeon does. The patient 'receives' it: shujutsu o ukeru.
The stairs take o as the route, not ni.
Gohan means a meal here, not only rice.
Takes ni, not o; ruuru o mamoru is the more casual choice.
No 'live up'; you answer (kotaeru) expectations, with ni.
Not masuku o kiru: small worn items (mask, watch, scarf, tie) just take suru, as in masuku shiteru. masuku o tsukeru is the announcement register.
'Look in' suggests ni; the mirror takes o.
'Turn' suggests mawaru; at corners it is magaru.
English 'side with' is a verb; Japanese says 'become an ally'
'make' is not tsukuru; decisions are handed down (kudasu)
'play' is not asobu; roles are fulfilled (hatasu)
Not popyuraa da: 'popular' is ninki ga aru ('has popularity'), and ninki nai for unpopular.
No 'dizzy' adjective: dizziness 'does', memai ga suru.
Not naisho o mamoru: 'keep it secret' is ni suru, as in kore naisho ni shite ne (himitsu ni suru is the more neutral twin).
Not ai kontakuto o suru: eyes 'meet' with au 合う (fit), not au 会う (meet a person).
'Healthy' sends learners to kenkou. For food and habits Japanese says karada ni ii ('good for the body'), and karada ni warui for the opposite.
Saying thanks is orei o iu; orei o suru means repaying with a gift or favour
Telling someone an address is oshieru, not iu
English 'it costs a lot' has no verb to copy: money kakaru, the same verb as time (kekkou kakatta).
Not ocha o tsukuru: tea and coffee are 'put in' (ireru), not made.
Not yuki ga ochiru: snow falls with furu, the same verb as rain.
Not terebi ni iru: a person on TV terebi ni deru ('comes out on'); a programme is terebi de yaru.
English 'shave' needs no object, but Japanese names what comes off: hige o soru (face), ashi no ke o soru (legs).
Money received from someone is morau, not eru.
'face' is not mukau here; you look at (miru) reality
Not kanashii or daun: 'you seem down' is genki nai ne. Genki ja nai sounds more like 'not healthy'.
Not chigai o iu or oshieru: here 'tell' is wakaru, and the difference is the subject. It is usually heard as chigai ga wakaranai.
Crossing takes o, not ni
Activity as purpose takes ni, no -ing form
Crossing takes o, not ni
One verb in English; Japanese needs noun + haku
Not megane o kiru or tsukeru: glasses 'hang' on the face, so the verb is kakeru.
Not inu o aruku, because aruku can't take the dog as its object. You go on the dog's walk: inu no sanpo ni iku, or inu o sanpo ni tsureteku.
Forms are put out (dasu), not 'filed'
'put on' splits by body part; coats take kiru
Hearing ability is kikoeru, not kiku
You enter (hairu) the main topic
Impression is received (ukeru), no passive needed
Granting a favour is kiku (listen), not suru
Not keshou o tsukeru or kiru: makeup takes suru. Many speakers say okeshou suru, and younger ones meiku suru.
Not okane o tsukuru: 'make money' is kasegu, 'earn'. Okane o tsukuru sounds like printing it or raising funds.
Following rules is shitagau with ni, not tsuite iku
Transitive akeru, not aku
English 'comfortable' about a place or group is igokochi ga ii, not just raku or kaiteki.
English 'take' works here. The trap is the contrast: a day off sick is shigoto o yasumu, while a planned break is yasumi o toru.
'Get an education' uses ukeru (receive), not morau.
'Have an attitude' is not motsu; Japanese takes toru.
'Dissatisfied' is a noun + aru; complaining aloud is monku o iu.
Emergency 'taken to hospital' is hakobareru, not tsurete ikareru.
The adjective 'considerate' is noun + aru in Japanese.
'I'm hungry' is a past-tense verb in Japanese: onaka ga hetta.
Personal habits and quirks are kuse, not shuukan.
'Attract' attention is atsumeru (gather), not hiku.
The path takes o (kaidan o oriru), and 'go down' is one verb, not iku.
'Have' a meal is toru or taberu, never motsu.
Not kutsu o toru: shoes and clothes come off with nugu, and toru sounds like picking them up.
Not adobaisu o ageru: to listen to someone's problem you 'ride on' it, soudan ni noru (to ask for advice is soudan suru).
Not tsuri o iku or tsuri suru ni iku: an activity noun takes ni iku directly (tsuri ni itta).

english: get tested, have a (medical) check or test
trap: Not kensa o suru, which is what the doctor does: the patient 'receives' a test, kensa o ukeru, as in shujutsu o ukeru.
Lower-body clothing takes haku, not kiru; pantsu usually means underwear.
'Use violence' is furuu (wield), not tsukau.
Helpful advice is sankou ni naru, not tasukeru.

english: appear in a dream; dream about (someone)
trap: English 'I dreamt about you' leads to translating 'about'. Japanese says the person came out in the dream: yume ni kimi ga dete kita.
'Be away' from home is rusu ni suru, not just inai.
'Right decision' is usually handan, not kettei.
'Smash to pieces' is konagona ni suru, not a single verb.
'Turn' at a corner is magaru, not mawaru.
Means making unreasonable demands, not saying 'impossible'.
Not densha o noru or densha o toru: you ride on a vehicle with ni noru, and 'take' is never toru here.
Not netsu o motteru: a fever 'exists', netsu ga aru (netsu aru mitai).
English 'come out/open' points to deru or hiraku. Flowers bloom with saku, and petals fall with chiru, not ochiru.
Personal bad habits are kuse, not shuukan.
Means a tasteless joke or 'this can't be real', not an unfunny one.
'Cause' trouble is okosu, not tsukuru.
'Watch' a game is just miru.
Accessories take suru (or hameru), not kiru.
'Mark' is noun + tsukeru; there is no single verb.
Not kado ni magaru: the corner takes o and the direction takes ni (tsugi no kado o migi ni magaru). 'Turn' is not mawaru (spin).
'I go to a Japanese school' as a routine is kayotteru, not itteru: iku is one trip, kayou is regular attendance.
English 'shed' has no match: tears are made to flow (nagasu).
No 'to': kiku takes the radio directly with o.

english: wait for someone to come home
trap: 'Wait for' takes o, not ni.
Dressing someone else is kiseru; kiru is only dressing yourself.
Not beruto o kiru: belts, watches and ties take suru.
English 'it smells' has no verb match: the scent 'does' (ga suru).

english: make one's dream come true, achieve a dream
trap: English 'achieve / realise a dream' pushes to tassei suru or jitsugen suru. The everyday verb is kanaeru, the transitive half of yume ga kanau.
Usually ni, not a bare object like English 'climb'.
'Get paid' is not a passive: you receive (morau) the salary.
Not takushii o toru: vehicles take noru with ni.
Careful planning 'kneads' (neru) the plan; tsukuru sounds flat.
English 'whistle' is one verb; Japanese blows (fuku) a noun.
Not michi o iu or michi o hanasu: telling someone the way is oshieru ('teach'), as in eki made no michi oshiete kuremasen ka?
Used with suru (tsurai omoi o suru = go through a hard time); omoi here is not 'thought'.
Not eigo o wakaru: wakaru takes ga.
Takes ni, not a bare object like English 'climb'.
Accidents 'arise' (okiru/okoru); being in one is jiko ni au.
You 'put out' (dasu) a conclusion, not reach it.
Not zubon o kiru: trousers, skirts, socks and tights take haku, like shoes (anything you step into).
Lights and the TV take tsukeru, but powering up a phone or PC is dengen o ireru ('put the power in').
okashii here means 'odd', not 'funny'.
Intransitive naru with ga; ringing it yourself is narasu.
Not tomodachi o tsukuru as the default: friends 'come into being' with ga dekiru (tomodachi dekita).
Not shinpai suru, which means you are the one worrying: worrying someone else is shinpai o kakeru (shinpai kakete gomen).
Not ruuru ni tsuite iku: following rules is mamoru ('protect'), like promises and time. Ruuru ni shitagau is stiffer.
Effort is 'hung' (kakeru), not taken (toru).
Events are 'opened' (hiraku), not held (motsu).
Lights and devices take tsukeru, not mawasu or ireru.
Not hima o motsu: free time 'exists' (ga aru).
Not denki o tomeru or shimeru: lights, TVs and heaters go off with kesu (put out).
English has no verb to translate: a hole 'opens' (ana ga aku). Making one is ana o akeru.

english: make fun of, look down on
trap: Not warau or anything with tsukuru: 'make fun of' is baka ni suru, literally 'treat as a fool'.
English 'attractive' is an adjective; Japanese says the person has charm.
'Come true' is the single verb kanau, not hontou ni naru.
Switches and power are cut (kiru), not erased (kesu) like lights.
'Finish' suggests owaru; for errands and business Japanese says you ga sumu.
Chuudoku also means poisoning; addiction to games etc. uses ni naru.
Kaori is for pleasant scents; nioi is neutral, kusai is bad.
Not kusuri ga hataraku: medicine 'takes effect', kusuri ga kiku, a homophone of kiku 'listen'.
Not seki o mamoru or tameru: saving a seat is 'taking' it, seki o toru. Totte oku means keeping it for later.
Okuru isn't the default here: posting a letter or card is tegami o dasu ('put it out'); the same goes for nengajou.
English 'unlock' is one verb; Japanese 'opens the key', kagi o akeru, the opposite of kagi o kakeru.

english: have things to talk about, click in conversation
trap: Here au means 'fit', not 'meet'. People whose conversation fits are hanashi ga au; ki ga au is the separate idiom.
Bones snap (oru), not break like objects (kowasu); also means take pains.
Not sayonara o iu; people say (o)wakare o iu.
'Get a message' is not morau here; a passed-on message is heard (kiku).
'Take' tempts toru; risks are usually borne (ou), though risuku o toru exists.
English 'water' is a verb; Japanese 'gives' water, (hana ni) mizu o yaru, or politely ageru.
Not gitaa o suru: guitar takes hiku like the piano (gitaa hikeru? = can you play guitar?).
Not shokuyoku o motte inai: an appetite ga aru or ga nai.
'Make a good impression' is ii inshou o ataeru, not tsukuru.
'I have a bad feeling' is warui yokan ga suru, not motsu.
'Miss' is not sabishii or noriokureru; chances are let slip (nogasu).
'Carry' tempts hakobu; carrying a bag is motsu.
Not denki o mawasu or akeru: lights are tsukeru'd, and denki here means the light itself.
'Make trouble' is not tsukuru; trouble is raised (okosu).
English 'motivated' is an adjective; Japanese has (or lacks) yaruki.

english: become the talk of the town
trap: English passive 'be talked about' becomes X ga wadai ni naru.
Not jikan o korosu: killing time is tsubusu, 'crush' (kafe de jikan tsubushiteta).
Not chiimu o sanka suru: you 'enter' a team, club or circle with ni hairu (saakuru ni haitta).
English 'cause a fuss' makes learners want a transitive verb; Japanese says the situation becomes a fuss.
English 'be honest' points to shoujiki; for speaking your true feelings people say honne o iu.
English 'get water' suggests toru or morau; scooping water up from a source or tap into a container is kumu.
English 'everyone is here' leads to zenin iru; for a group that has all gathered people say zenin sorotta.
English 'give' suggests ageru; with impressions Japanese uses ataeru.
The stairs take o (the path you move along), not ni.
English 'shatter' has no single verb here; Japanese says it becomes pieces.
English 'close' suggests shimeru; holes and gaps are blocked with fusagu.

english: has a nice ring to it
trap: English 'sounds good' leads to yosasou; for how a name or word sounds people say ii hibiki.
English 'mean' has no direct adjective; Japanese says the disposition is bad (also ijiwaru).
English 'come and cheer' leads to kite ouen suru; Japanese puts the purpose noun with ni kuru.
English 'agree' points to sansei suru; for two people sharing views Japanese says opinions match.
English 'kneel' has no single verb; Japanese puts the knee down with tsuku.
Dictionaries give i for 'stomach', but an everyday tummy ache is onaka ga itai, not i ga itai.
Not okane o harau: paying back a loan is kaesu, 'give back' (ashita kaesu ne).
English 'buy/get insurance' leads to kau; Japanese enters insurance with ni hairu.
English 'it costs' has the thing as subject; Japanese makes the expense the subject with ga kakaru.
English 'reach a conclusion' suggests tsuku; Japanese says the conclusion comes out (ga deru, or o dasu).
English 'get sleep' suggests eru or morau; Japanese takes sleep with toru.
English 'tell apart' is something you do; Japanese says the distinction attaches (ga tsuku), mostly in the negative.
Transitive narasu for ringing it yourself; naru is the bell ringing on its own.
English 'uncomfortable' points to physical discomfort; for an awkward place or situation it's igokochi ga warui.
English 'on the sofa' leads to no ue ni; the place of sleeping takes de.
Not atama o tataku (that's hitting on purpose): banging your head into something is butsukeru, as in tana ni atama butsuketa.

english: can make it, can fit it in
trap: Not tsugou ga dekiru: an arrangement 'attaches' (tsuku). Example: tsugou tsuitara renraku shite.
English 'short-staffed' has no direct word; Japanese says hands are not enough.
The person you ask takes ni, not o (honnin ni kiku), and kiku is also 'listen'.
English 'form/make a team' leads to tsukuru; teams and pairs are put together with kumu.
English 'take advice' leads to toru; Japanese listens to advice with kiku.
'Gain' is not eru here; experience is piled up (tsumu).
'Take off' clothes is nugu, not toru.
English 'I have news' pushes toward motsu; Japanese says oshirase ga aru.
'Sign' a contract is musubu 'tie', not sain suru.
'Adopt' has no single verb; you make the child your youshi (youshi ni suru).
'Follow' rules is mamoru 'protect/keep', not a verb of following.
'Stand in line' is just narabu; no tatsu.
Going on stage is agaru 'go up', not iku.
English 'tea' usually means koucha; ocha means green tea by default in Japan.

english: get through (on the phone), reach someone
trap: 'I can't reach him' isn't todokanai or aenai: it's denwa ga tsunagaranai.
Not only harau: offering to pay or chip in is watashi ga dasu yo ('I'll put the money out').
Regular attendance is kayou; iku sounds like a single trip.
'Good taste' is shumi (also 'hobby') ga ii, not aji, which is flavour.
'Make' an appointment is toru 'take', not tsukuru.
You close it with shimeru; shimaru is the window closing by itself.
'Get' cancer is naru 'become', not motsu or toru.
'Ask' someone to dinner is sasou with ni, not kiku.
'Panic' as a verb is panikku o okosu or panikku ni naru, not panikku suru.
'Put up for sale' is uri ni dasu 'put out to selling', not just uru.
'Have symptoms' is shoujou ga deru 'come out', not motsu.
'Go out for dinner' is just gohan (ni) iku; no taberu needed.
English 'windy' is one adjective. Japanese says the wind is strong: kaze ga tsuyoi, not kaze ga ooi.
Not terebi o akeru or on ni suru: screens, like lights, are tsukeru'd, and off is kesu.
'Live a ... life' is ~na kurashi o suru, not ikiru.
ashi covers both foot and leg; 'my feet hurt' is still ashi ga itai.
'Get' a tattoo is ireru 'put in', not morau or suru.
'Have a baby' is akachan ga umareru 'is born', not motsu.
naosu is curing it; 'I got better' is byouki ga naotta.
'Turn off' a light is kesu 'erase/put out', not ofu ni suru.
seki is a noun; to cough is seki o suru (or seki ga deru).
'Achieve' results is ageru 'raise', not eru or tsukuru.
Not hoteru ni iru or sutei suru: staying the night is tomaru, the same sound as a car stopping.
Easy to guess once fuku is known. The risk is the homophones: kaze means wind or a cold, and fuku means blow or wipe. Keep it apart from kaze o hiku (catch a cold).
Not piano o suru or asobu: keyboard and string instruments take hiku (piano hiiteru).
Not denwa o morau: an incoming call 'hangs' on you (denwa ga kakatte kuru). It is the intransitive of denwa o kakeru.
'Something came up at work' is shigoto ga haitchatta (work 'entered' the schedule), not okiru or kuru.
Not denwa o morau: a call comes in, so it's denwa ga kakatte kita (casually just denwa kita).
Break in is not kowasu; a burglar simply 'enters' (hairu), and dorobou ni hairareta = we got burgled.
Have a headache is not motsu; the headache is the subject: zutsuu ga hidoi / zutsuu ga suru.
Put on is not kiru or tsukeru; switching a call mode is X ni suru.
Cover is not kabuseru or oou; ears are blocked: fusagu.
Take off is not nugu; masks, glasses and accessories are hazusu.
Leave is not deru or oite iku; a note left for someone is nokosu.
Make is not tsukuru; errors are okasu (casually just machigaeru).
No dekiru needed; mostly heard negative: yosou ga tsukanai = can't tell what will happen.
Come back is not kaeru or modoru; memories revive: yomigaeru.
Not yoyaku o tsukuru: you 'take' a booking (yoyaku toreta? = did you get one?). Plain yoyaku suru also works.
Win is not katsu; prizes are taken: shou o toru (or morau).
Close is not chikai (physically near); close friends are shitashii.
Appear is not arawareru; being printed is noru (載る).
Cold is not samui (weather); cold to the touch or drink is tsumetai.
Take is not toru here; attending a class is ukeru (toru means signing up).
Keep is not motsu; distance is maintained: tamotsu (or kyori o oku).
No passive verb needed; being expelled is taigaku ni naru.
Turn off pulls toward kesu (lights); engines are kiru.
Rise pulls toward agaru; the sun noboru (casually hi ga noboru).
Have is not motsu; body marks use ga aru.
Have is not motsu; the attack itself occurs: hossa ga okiru.
Take off is not nugu; belts and seatbelts are hazusu.
Not hone ga kowareru: bones, sticks and umbrellas 'snap' (oreru). Kowareru is for machines.
Keep is not motsu; balance is toru.
Arrive pulls toward tsuku; mail and parcels todoku.
Doraibu means a leisure drive, not driving itself (unten suru).
Not se ga mijikai: short in height is hikui (low). Mijikai is only for length.
Swapped with kariru: kashite = lend me; karite ii? = can I borrow?

english: be expecting a baby, get pregnant
trap: Not akachan o motsu: 'we're having a baby' is akachan ga dekita (a baby 'came into being').
Japanese has no word for 'flush': you make the toilet 'flow' (nagasu), as in toire nagashite or mizu o nagasu.
English says 'likely'; Japanese says the probability is high.
English uses a verb (don't get along); Japanese says the relationship is bad.
Approach takes ni, not o.

english: be immune; be used to it
trap: English uses an adjective; Japanese says you 'have immunity'.
kippu is a train ticket; concert tickets are chiketto.
baiku means motorbike, not bicycle; noru takes ni.
Japanese 'heads toward' the goal, usually mokuhyou ni mukatte ganbaru.
English 'goes off'; Japanese says the alarm rings (naru).
Drums are hit (tataku), not hiku like other instruments.
Not shiken ni shippai suru: failing an exam is 'falling', ochiru with ni (ukatta / ochita).

english: the call drops, get cut off
trap: Not denwa ga ochiru: a dropped call is denwa ga kireta, the intransitive half of denwa o kiru.
'Tear up' has no verb to copy: tears come out, so namida deta. Naku is crying outright.
'Put in' is ni ireru, not oku.
English uses one adjective; Japanese says the will is strong.
'Pull' here is nuku, not hiku.
Errands 'get settled' (sumu); owaru is less typical.
Casual grumbling is monku o iu; kujou is a formal complaint.
Heavy breathing is 'rough breath' (arai), not omoi.
Speed is 'put out' (dasu), not raised or made.
In speech people just say seikou suru.
Not netsu o morau or eru: a fever 'comes out', netsu ga deru (netsu deta).
Not shigoto o toru or shigoto ni ikanai: missing work is yasumu ('rest') with o, the same for school (gakkou o yasumu).
Not boushi o hazusu: hats come off with toru (boushi o nugu also works), not with the accessory verb hazusu.
Not kyanseru sareru for events: rained-off matches and cancelled events chuushi ni naru. Postponed is enki ni naru.

english: how much it comes to (in total)
trap: A total isn't 'is' but 'becomes': zenbu de ikura ni naru? asks the total, and every cashier says sen-en ni narimasu.
Not ame ga tomaru or owaru, and not yameru (a person quitting): rain stops with intransitive yamu.
Not me ga yowai or 'warui me ga aru': poor eyesight is me ga warui (shiryoku is the formal word).
Not sutoresu ni naru: stress 'piles up' (tamaru).
English uses one verb; Japanese needs ibiki + kaku, the same kaku as ase o kaku (sweat).
Landing a job is usually intransitive, shigoto ga mitsukatta (a job turned up). English 'I found' pushes toward shigoto o mitsuketa, which sounds less natural.
Scores are 'taken', not received: hyakuten totta, ii ten toreta (not ten o morau).

english: get the hang of it, get the knack
trap: The set phrase is kotsu o tsukamu ('grab the knack'). Kotsu ga wakaru is also heard, but kotsu o toru is not.
Not menkyo o morau: you 'take' a licence by earning it (menkyo totta). The same goes for qualifications: shikaku o toru.
Not 'hayai rannaa': a fast runner is ashi ga hayai ('legs are fast'). Ashi ga osoi is slow.
Not takarakuji ni katsu: you don't beat a lottery. The ticket 'hits' with ataru, and the lottery is the subject. The same goes for raffles and prize draws (kuji ga ataru).
English 'graduate' leads to sotsugyou suru (fine but stiff). In conversation people say daigaku deta ('left university').
Not takarakuji ni katsu: you don't beat a lottery, it hits you. 'Takarakuji atattara...' (also ga ataru).

english: there are a lot of them

trap: Not asobu: playing music from a speaker is ongaku o kakeru; asobu is play as in have fun, hiku is play an instrument.
Not shiken o toru: you 'receive' an exam, ukeru (also tesuto o ukeru, mensetsu o ukeru, and daigaku o ukeru for sitting a university's entrance exam).
Not tsuku: a dead phone that 'won't turn on' is dengen ga hairanai.
Learners swap kariru (borrow) and kasu (lend). The lender takes ni or kara (tomodachi ni karita).
Not 'nagai kami ga aru' for 'she has long hair': say kanojo wa kami ga nagai.
Not se ga sodatsu: 'you've grown!' is se nobita ne (or ookiku natta ne).
Not jugyou o nuku or tobasu: skipping class or work is saboru (from 'sabotage'), while skipping a meal is nuku.
Not gasorin o kau or morau: fuel is 'put in' (ireru), as in gasorin irete kara iku.
English 'fit' has no one-word verb: say saizu ga au / awanai. This au means 'match' and sounds the same as au 'meet'.
Not okane o tasukeru or setsuyaku suru: saving up is tameru, 'pile up' (setsuyaku means cutting back).
Not yotei ga kuru or deru: a plan that gets booked 'enters' (sono hi yotei haitteru = I've got something that day).
There's no adjective for 'motivated': motivation 'comes out' (yaruki ga deru, or yaruki ga denai).
Learners reach for hagu or toru. Peeling the skin off fruit or vegetables is muku, as in mikan no kawa o muku.
Not mimi ga kikoenai: the plain, polite way is 'far ears' (mimi ga tooi), the mirror of me ga warui.

english: not be in the mood, not feel like it
trap: Nothing in 'I don't feel like it' leads to noru (ride). The plain way to say it is ki ga noranai.
Mostly guessable from yameru = quit. The catch is that you quit the company or the job (kaisha/shigoto o yameru), and 辞める sounds identical to 止める 'stop'.
Not shumi o motsu in speech: having a hobby is ga aru (nanka shumi aru?), like jikan ga aru.
Not kami o migaku: teeth are brushed with migaku, hair with tokasu.

english: get hit / run over by a car
trap: Not kuruma ni utareru: being run over is hikareru, the passive of hiku, which sounds the same as the hiku in kaze o hiku.
No English pairing to copy. 'Do you like the food here?' is asked as nihon no tabemono, kuchi ni au? Here au means 'fit', not 'meet'.
Not hataraku or ugoku: 'the Wi-Fi isn't working' is netto ga tsunagaranai ('doesn't connect').
Not kareshi o eru or morau: a partner 'comes into being' with ga dekiru (kanojo dekita!).

english: have good taste / a good eye (style)
trap: English 'good taste' leads to aji (flavour). Taste in clothes, music or gifts is sensu ga ii; shumi ga ii is also used.

english: get some exercise, move your body
trap: Not only undou suru: the casual 'I need some exercise' is karada o ugokasu.
Not gomi o toru or motte iku: taking out the trash is gomi o dasu (put it out).
Not yubiwa o kiru: things you push a finger or hand into (rings, gloves) take hameru. yubiwa shiteru is also common for wearing one.
English 'the snow is sticking/settling' has no match: snow piles up, tsumoru, not tsuku or nokoru.
Not netsu ga oriru or heru: a fever 'drops', netsu ga sagaru (netsu sagatta?).
Attending a class is deru with ni. jugyou o deru would mean walking out of it, and shusseki suru is the formal word.
Not shiai o suru for 'play in the game': taking part is deru (nichiyou shiai deru), and so is taikai ni deru (enter a tournament).
Not fue o hiku or suru: wind instruments are blown with fuku, the verb of kaze ga fuku (the wind blows).
False friend: sutairu ga ii means a good figure (slim, well-proportioned), not good fashion sense. Fashion is oshare.
Not kopii o tsukuru: copies are 'taken' with toru. Kopii suru is also used.
Not youji ga kuru: 'something came up' is kyuu ni youji ga dekita. Youji ga aru means 'I have things to do'.
Not hige o sodateru or nobasu: facial hair is 'made to sprout' (hayasu), the transitive of haeru. hige haeteru hito = a man with a beard.

english: be compatible, go well together (people, also food pairings)
trap: 'We're compatible' has no Japanese verb to copy. You say the match is good, aishou ga ii (also wain to chiizu wa aishou ga ii).

english: do someone a favour (agree to a request)
trap: Not onegai o suru, which means making the request. Doing the favour is onegai o kiku (chotto onegai kiite kureru?).

english: run a shop, bar or restaurant
trap: Not hashiru or motsu. Running a shop is yaru (oya ga izakaya yatteru); keiei suru is formal.
Not toire o tsukau: asking to use someone's toilet is 'borrowing' it (toire karite mo ii?).
'Silent mode' is the made-in-Japan manaa moodo ('manner mode') with ni suru, not sairento ni oku.
The candidate ukeru (receives) the interview, like shiken o ukeru; mensetsu o suru means you are the one interviewing.

english: hot water comes out / runs (tap, shower)
trap: 'There's no hot water' is oyu ga denai, not oyu ga nai. This is the intransitive of mizu o dasu / oyu o dasu.
'Work for X' is not X no tame ni hataraku: say X ni tsutometeru (or X de hataraiteru), with ni and almost always in the -te iru form.

english: a shop opens (for the day), is open
trap: Not mise ga akeru or hiraku: 'is it open?' is aiteru? or nanji made aiteru?. Mise o hiraku means opening a new shop.
Not takushii o toru or takushii o tsukamu: hailing one in the street is hirou ('pick up'). tsukamaeru also works; phoning for one is yobu.
Not seki o ageru: offering your seat to someone is yuzuru ('hand over').
English 'an earthquake hit/struck' has no matching verb. Say jishin ga okiru (casually jishin ga atta / kita). The shaking itself is yureru.
Not samui kaze by default: wind you feel on your skin is tsumetai (cold to the touch). Samui describes the air or how you feel.
English 'clean your room' leads to souji suru, which means scrubbing and vacuuming. Putting things away is katazukeru.
Not uso ga mitsukaru: lies and secrets 'come out' with bareru (casual), as in uso bareta.

english: put something off, deal with it later
trap: 'Put off' has no Japanese verb to copy. You turn the task into 'later', atomawashi ni suru.
Not kaigi o deru (= leave the meeting room) or kaigi ni sanka suru in casual speech: attending is ni deru.
Not michi ni wataru or kurosu suru: what you cross takes o (michi, hashi, shingou o wataru).
There is no word for 'seconds' or 'refill' to translate; it is the noun okawari, used with suru or on its own (okawari kudasai).
English 'it thunders' is one verb. Japanese makes the thunder sound: kaminari ga naru (鳴る 'ring', a homophone of naru 'become').
Not samui alone: chills 'do', samuke ga suru; samui means the room is cold.
Shots are 'hit', chuusha o utsu; as the patient say chuusha utte moratta or utareta.

english: expire, go past the use-by date
trap: There's no verb for 'expire': the deadline 'snaps' with kireru. For food, people say shoumi kigen ga kireteru. Passports and cards just say kigen ga kireta.
Not nimotsu ga tsuku: deliveries 'reach' you, so nimotsu todoita. Tsuku is for people and vehicles arriving.

english: be a good person, have a nice personality
trap: 'He's nice' is usually seikaku ga ii or yasashii; seikaku ga warui means mean or nasty.
Not juutai de tomaru: you 'fall into' traffic (hamaru), the same verb as geemu ni hamaru (get hooked).
A bruise dekiru (forms), not tsuku; usually aza dekichatta.
Not tokei o kiru: a watch takes suru (tokei shiteru). tsukeru also works but sounds stiffer.
English 'iron' is a verb; Japanese says airon o kakeru, not airon suru.
Not ichinichi ga nagai, which means 'it was a long day': daylight hours are hi ga nagai / hi ga mijikai.
No 'sore' adjective: the throat hurts, nodo ga itai.
Not shingou: phone signal is denpa ('radio waves'); shingou is a traffic light.
Not petto ga aru or petto o motsu: you keep an animal with kau (飼う), which sounds exactly like kau, 'buy'.
'Punctual' is an adjective in English, but Japanese 'protects the time': jikan mamotte ne.
Like kami o kiru, you say you dyed your hair even when the salon did it. kinpatsu ni someru = go blond.

english: be in a photo, appear in a picture
trap: Not shashin ni iru or haitte iru: appearing in a photo is utsuru, as in kono shashin ni utsutteru no dare?
Not koe ga fukai: a deep voice is low, hikui. A high-pitched one is koe ga takai.
Not seki ga furii or seki ga hima: a free seat is aiteru ('open'), as in koko aitemasu ka?
Not ikura kakaru for a price tag: what an item costs takes suru (kore ikura shita? = how much was this?); kakaru is for running costs of a trip or service.
Not suupu o taberu: soup and miso soup are drunk (nomu), even with a spoon.

english: get an upset stomach, get diarrhoea
trap: English 'have an upset stomach' gives no usable verb. Japanese 'breaks' the stomach with kowasu, transitive, with the speaker as subject: onaka kowashita.
False friend: tenshon means excitement or energy, not stress. 'I'm excited' is tenshon agaru, and tenshon takai means hyper.
Not denki ga kesu: the intransitive is kieru, and 'the light is off' is denki kieteru.
Not hana o fuku: fuku is for blowing air, wind or a flute. You blow your nose with kamu, which sounds like kamu, 'bite'.
No 'addictive' adjective is used for snacks: you say kuse ni naru ('it becomes a habit').
Not okane o tsukau when you mean putting money into something: fuku ni okane o kakeru. It's the transitive half of okane ga kakaru.

english: get dirt or a stain off, clean it off
trap: English 'get off' or 'remove' suggests toru; the usual verb is otosu (drop), as in keshou o otosu.
Not pakku suru or nimotsu o ireru: packing a bag is tsumeru, 'cram in' (mou nimotsu tsumeta?). nimotsu o matomeru means 'get your stuff together'.
Not jiyuu: being free is aku, 'to open up' (ashita aiteru? = are you free tomorrow?).
Not warui kaze: a bad cold is hidoi kaze; warui means wrong or at fault.
Not mizu o kesu: kesu is for lights, the TV and fire. Water and gas are stopped with tomeru. To turn the tap on: mizu o dasu.
Japanese has no verb for 'sober up': being drunk 'wears off' (sameru), the same verb as me ga sameru.

english: send (something) for repair, get it fixed
trap: English 'get it fixed' has no verb to translate; Japanese sends it out: sumaho o shuuri ni dasu.

english: get a bonus (a bonus is paid out)
trap: The usual line is that the bonus deru (comes out): boonasu deta? Boonasu o morau is also fine.
Not kami ga ochiru: hair coming out (in the shower, from stress, with age) is nukeru. Ochiteru is only for a hair lying on the floor.
Not kaminari ga utsu: lightning falls (ochita). Kaminari ga naru is the thunder you hear.
Not nikki o motsu or tamotsu: keeping a diary or any record is tsukeru, as in kakeibo o tsukeru (keep household accounts).
Not megane o nugu: nugu is only for clothes and shoes. Glasses, watches, masks, rings and earrings come off with hazusu.
Not sakkaa o asobu: asobu means playing around, so sports take suru (casually yaru: sakkaa yatteru).
Not shiai o katsu: English 'win the game' is transitive, but Japanese wins at it with ni (geemu ni katta).
Not ka ni kamareru: mosquitoes and bees 'sting' with sasu, used in the passive. Kamu is for dogs and snakes.
Not denpa o morau: having signal is denpa ga hairu, and 'no signal' is denpa hairanai.
Not michi ga isogashii (busy is for people) or kuruma ga ooi: crowded roads, trains and shops are konderu.
Not jikan o jiyuu ni suru: clearing time for someone is akeru (ashita akete oku ne).
'Get wet' is the single verb nureru, with no 'get' or naru added. The rain takes ni (ame de nureta is also heard).
English 'connect' covers both: you tsunagu a device (waifai ni tsunaide), but the net tsunagaru on its own.
Handing in is dasu ('put out'), not ageru or teishutsu suru in speech. When a teacher says it, dasu means 'set homework'.
Not torihada o morau or ga deru: goosebumps 'stand up' with tatsu, and the noun is the subject. It covers cold, fear and being moved.
English gives no hint of kuzusu ('crumble'). Learners say byouki ni naru, which sounds like a real illness rather than being run down.
Not tamago o kowasu: eggs, glasses and plates 'split' (waru).

english: visit someone in hospital, visit a sick person
trap: Not byouin o tazuneru or houmon suru: visiting a sick person is omimai ni iku.
Not chiketto o morau: securing tickets is chiketto o toru, and toreta! means 'I got them'.
Not hi o morau: sunlight 'hits', so a sunny room is hi ga ataru heya.
'Empty' has no verb form; say kara ni suru (make empty).
Not koeru: the cold itself 'heals', kaze ga naoru (kaze naotta?); you cure it with kaze o naosu.
Not terebi ni aru: 'the film is on TV tonight' is konban terebi de yaru ('TV is doing it'); ni deru is for people.
There's no English verb to translate: breath 'runs out' (kireru), the same verb as juuden ga kireru.

english: the conversation gets lively, have a great chat
trap: No English verb fits: talk and parties 'swell up' (moriagaru), as in sugoi moriagatta ne.
English 'take' leads to motte iku; natives say dasu (send out), the same pattern as shuuri ni dasu.
Not hanashi ga kawaru or hanareru: a conversation that drifts 'veers off' (soreru), and hanashi o modosu brings it back.
'Sigh' is a verb in English. Japanese uses a noun with tsuku, the same verb as uso o tsuku.

english: black out; one's memory goes blank (from drinking)
trap: Not kioku o nakusu (amnesia, formal): blacking out from drink is kioku ga tobu (nomisugite kioku tonda).
'Fall' asleep is tsuku (or just nemuru), not ochiru.
There's no separate verb for 'tan' or 'burn': the skin is 'grilled by the sun', hi ni yakeru, the same yakeru as niku ga yakeru.

english: take / drop someone to the station, see someone off
trap: Not just eki made tsurete iku: walking or driving someone somewhere is okuru (the 'send' verb), as in okutte iku yo.
Not eki o tsuku or eki ni kita for 'I'm here': arriving is tsuku with ni, as in ima eki tsuita.
English splits grill, roast, bake, toast and fry; Japanese uses yaku for all dry-heat cooking (pan o yaku = make toast).
Not kami ga sodatsu: hair grows = nobiru. 'Your hair's grown' is kami nobita ne.
Not tsumoru (that's for snow): work, chores and laundry pile up with tamaru.

english: ruin one's health, make oneself ill (from overwork)
trap: English 'ruin your health' gives no verb; Japanese breaks the body: muri suru to karada kowasu yo.
A smell clinging to clothes tsuku (sticks), like shimi ga tsuku: yakiniku no nioi ga fuku ni tsuita.
Not suibun o nomu: you 'take in' fluids, suibun o toru, just as you say eiyou o toru for nutrition.

english: stick in one's mind, be memorable
trap: Not oboeyasui or kioku suru: 'the most memorable part was…' is ichiban inshou ni nokotta no wa…
Not kyuuryou o morau, which is just 'get paid': a raise is the salary going up, kyuuryou agatta.
Not deeta o nakusu: files and photos disappear, kieru (shashin zenbu kiechatta). Kesu is deleting them yourself.
Not taijuu o tsukeru or eru: weight is the subject and it increases, taijuu ga fueru. To lose weight is taijuu ga heru, or simply yaseru.
Not densha ga osoi: osoi means slow, and a train running late is okureteru. Switching ga to ni flips it to 'I missed the train'.
Not densha o misu shita or densha o nakushita: missing a train is ni okureru (casually also nogashita or noriokureta).
Not kuruma de byouki ni naru: motion sickness uses you, the verb for getting drunk (kuruma yoi, fune ni you).
Same tsukeru as lights, and eakon o kakeru (run it) is equally natural; not on ni suru or mawasu.
Not taiko o hiku or suru: drums are hit, tataku, and a drum kit works the same way (doramu o tataku).
Not 'sugu byouki ni naru hito' as the default: 'gets sick a lot' is karada ga yowai. Karada ga joubu is the sturdy opposite.
Not kabi ni naru: mould 'grows' the way hair does (haeru).
There's no adjective for 'fit': stamina is something you have or lack (tairyoku aru, tairyoku nai).
Not just yotei ga ippai: a full schedule is 'stuffed' (tsumaru), like a blocked nose. Example: raishuu wa yotei ga tsumatteru.

english: have the same tastes, share interests
trap: English 'we share hobbies' points to a sharing verb, but Japanese says your tastes 'match' (au), as in saizu ga au.

english: be perceptive, quick to catch on, have good instincts
trap: English 'sharp' leads to atama ga ii, which means clever. Picking up on things is kan ga ii.

english: run a fever, come down with a fever (of a person, often a child)
trap: Not netsu o morau: with the person as subject it is netsu o dashita (musuko ga netsu dashite). Netsu ga deta is the same event from the fever's side.
English uses the adjective 'stiff'; Japanese uses the verb koru: kata ga kotteru.
Not kaze o ageru: you 'transfer' a cold, kaze o utsusu (kaze utsushichatta, gomen).
Not shiai o nakusu: losing a contest is makeru (losing an object is nakusu), and it takes ni, never o (shiai ni maketa).
Not piano o benkyou suru or ressun o toru: lessons with a teacher are narau (kodomo no koro piano naratteta).
Not tebukuro o kiru: gloves 'fit on' (hameru), like rings; tebukuro o suru is also everyday.
Not michi o tanomu or michi o shitsumon suru: asking the way is kiku, the verb for listening.
Not jikan ni tsuku or dekiru: making it in time is maniau, with ni on the deadline or train (densha ni maniatta).
Not mizu o niru: you boil 'hot water' (oyu), and the verb is wakasu; niru is for cooking food.
Intransitive half: 'the kettle's boiled' is oyu ga waita, not oyu ga wakashita.
Not taiyou ga tsuyoi or taiyou ga atsui: strong sun is hizashi (sunlight) ga tsuyoi.
No 'stuffy' adjective: the nose clogs, hana ga tsumaru (hana tsumatteru).
A topic that's on the test 'comes out' in it, kore tesuto ni deru?, not shiken ni aru.
Not kami ga hikui: hair length is mijikai. Hikui is only for height (se ga hikui).
Not mezamashi ga deru or ga iku: alarms, phones and bells ring with naru (鳴る), which sounds like naru, 'become'.

english: a stain or dirt comes out
trap: Not yogore ga deru: stains 'fall off', so kono shimi ochinai. Removing them is yogore o otosu.
Not shimi o morau: a stain 'attaches', so shimi tsuichatta. Getting it out uses ochiru.
Not just atatakai fuku o kiru: 'wrap up warm' is one noun, atsugi ('thick wearing'), plus suru.
The stomach rings: naru (鳴る), the verb for a phone or alarm, not the naru that means 'become'.

english: get a belly, have a paunch
trap: English 'get a gut' or 'put on weight' gives no clue: the belly deru (sticks out), usually onaka dete kita.
Not botan o shimeru or kakeru: buttons are tomeru (fasten); undoing them is hazusu.

english: a queue forms, there's a line
trap: Not gyouretsu ga aru: a queue 'comes into being', gyouretsu ga dekiteru. Joining it is narabu.
Not kinniku o tsukuru. Muscle is 'attached' with tsukeru, the transitive half of kinniku ga tsuku.

english: join a company, start working at a company
trap: English 'join a company' pushes to sanka suru (take part). Joining a firm, school or club is hairu: kaisha ni haitte sannen.
Not okane o toru: cash from the bank or ATM is orosu, 'bring down' (dasu also works casually).
Not omoi ame: heavy rain is strong rain, ame ga tsuyoi / tsuyoi ame (or ame ga hidoi). Omoi is only for weight.
Not shiken o pasu suru: passing is a verb English gives no hint of, ukaru, and the exam takes ni, not o (also daigaku ni ukatta).
Not hirou or toru: you pick a person up by going 'to meet' them, mukae ni iku. When they come for you: mukae ni kuru.

english: reply to a message or email
trap: Not meeru ni kotaeru: replying to a text is kaesu, 'send back' (LINE kaeshite, henji kaesu). kotaeru is for answering questions.
Not keshou o nugu or toru: makeup is 'dropped' with otosu, the same verb used for dirt and stains.
Not michi ga karappo or michi ga hima: an uncrowded road or train is suiteru, the same suku as in onaka ga suku.
When the money is the subject the verb is tamaru (okane tamattara = once I've saved up), not transitive tameru.
Not yotei o tsukuru or oku: you 'put in' a plan (raishuu ni ireta = I put it in for next week).
Not kami o kawaku or fuku: drying it yourself is the transitive kawakasu, while kami ga kawaku means it dries.
'Cough' is a verb in English; in Japanese the cough comes out, seki ga deru (seki ga tomaranai).
Not hana ga hashiru: 'nose water comes out', hanamizu ga deru.
Not kami o sodateru: growing your hair out is nobasu ('lengthen'), e.g. ima kami nobashiteru.

english: sleep lightly, be a light sleeper
trap: Not karui nemuri: sleep is 'shallow', asai. Deep sleep is nemuri ga fukai.
Not senaka ga itai: 'bad back' pain sits in the koshi (lower back and hips). Senaka is the upper back.
Not tsukare ga naoru: tiredness 'comes off' (toreru). It isn't cured.
There's no verb for 'scratch': a scratch 'attaches' (kizu ga tsuku).
Not only nakusu: losing a wallet or phone while out is usually otosu ('drop'), and the police ask where you dropped it.
Not isha o miru (that means looking at the doctor): to see a doctor is isha ni kakaru, or isha ni mite morau.
Not sakujo suru in speech: 'delete that photo!' is sono shashin keshite. Kesu means erase as well as switch off.
Not mise ga aku (that's opening for the day): a shop that has just opened is atarashii mise ga dekita.
Not kusuri o nomu or tsukeru: creams, ointment and sunscreen are 'spread' on (nuru); nomu is only for swallowing.
English 'unplug' is one verb; Japanese pulls out the konsento (plug/socket). Plugging in is konsento ni sasu.

english: a bug turns up (in the house)
trap: Not mushi ga iru for the moment of seeing it: pests (and ghosts) 'come out', gokiburi ga deta!

english: have a meal now, make it mealtime
trap: English 'let's eat' pushes to gohan o tabeyou. At home people say sorosoro gohan ni shiyou (let's switch to the meal), and ofuro ni suru? gohan ni suru? asks which comes first.
Not densha o tsukamaeru or densha o toru: making a train in time is ni maniau ('be in time for').
Not mezamashi o oku or setto suru: alarms are kakeru'd, like locks and vacuum cleaners.
Not denki o tsukeru when nobody's doing it: 'the light is on' is denki ga tsuiteru.
Not kasa o tsukau, hiraku or motsu: holding an umbrella over yourself is sasu. Kasa o hiraku only means opening it, and kasa o motsu means carrying it.
Not shinu: the plain way to say a dead phone is juuden kireta ('the charge ran out'); sumaho shinda is only a joke.
Not nekutai o kiru: a tie is 'tightened' with shimeru, which sounds like shimeru 'close'. Wearing one is just nekutai shiteru.
Not densha ga yameru: yameru is quitting. A train stopping (at a station, or halted) is tomaru.
Checking the seasoning is aji o miru ('look at the taste') or ajimi suru; ajiwau means savour.
Not netsu o toru: you 'measure' a fever, netsu o hakaru (netsu hakatta?).
Not ashi ga neru or nemuru: a numb, tingling foot is shibireru.

english: the AC is working (cooling or heating properly)
trap: Not ugoku: for an AC that is running but not cooling, Japanese says it doesn't kiku (take effect), as in kusuri ga kiku. Usually eakon kiitenai.

english: be online, be posted on the internet
trap: Not netto ni aru: being posted or listed is noru (載る), the same sound as getting on a train. Usually netto ni notteru.

english: feel heavy and run-down, feel sluggish
trap: Not just tsukareta: the heavy, achy feeling of a cold coming on is karada ga darui.
Not oru, which is for paper or snapping something. Clothes, laundry, futons and umbrellas are tatamu.
English 'rest up / recover' has no noun. Japanese 'takes off' the tiredness: onsen de tsukare o toru, yukkuri yasunde tsukare totte ne.

english: a typhoon is coming, a typhoon hits
trap: English 'a typhoon hits' pushes to ataru or utsu. Japanese says the typhoon comes: ashita taifuu kuru rashii yo.
Not paama o suru or morau: a perm takes kakeru, like an iron (airon o kakeru). At the salon it is paama o kakete morau.

english: the alcohol kicks in; start to feel drunk
trap: English 'it's hitting me' has no verb a learner could map. Feeling the drink kick in is yoi ga mawaru, also osake ga mawaru.
Not densha kara deru or densha ni oriru: getting off is oriru, with the vehicle marked by o (or kara).
Not samuku naru or tsumetaku naru: hot food or drink cooling off is sameru; samui is for weather and people.
Not osake o motenai: low tolerance is 'weak at alcohol' (osake ga/ni yowai).
Not aji ga yowai or aji ga nai: food short on salt is usui (thin), the same word as weak coffee.
Not tsuyoi koohii: coffee, tea and flavour are koi (dense) or usui (thin); tsuyoi is for alcohol.
Not watashi wa ippai: the stomach is what's full, onaka ippai.
Catching it from a person is kaze ga utsuru, not kaze o hiku (utsuru kara chikazukanaide).
Not tsukau or asobu: idly being on your phone is sumaho o ijiru ('fiddle with'); tsukau means using it for a task.
'Be into / hooked on' has no verb to translate, so learners fall back on suki desu. The native way is X ni hamatteru, with ni.
There is no adjective for 'athletic': say undou shinkei ga ii ('motor nerves are good'), not supootsu ga jouzu.
Not kanjou o wakeru: splitting the bill is the noun warikan + ni suru, literally 'make it warikan'. Warikan de ii? is the usual question.
Not mise ga tojiru: closing time is shimaru, as in mou shimatteru ('it's already closed'). Mise o shimeru is the owner closing up, and mise o tatamu is closing down for good.
Not konbini ni tomaru, which means staying the night there: dropping in on the way is yoru.
Not heya ga kitanai for clutter: messy is chirakatteru, and kitanai means dirty.
Not just mise ga ippai or hito ga ooi: busy restaurants and trains are konderu, and the opposite is suiteru.
English 'skip' pushes toward tobasu. Meals are 'pulled out': asagohan nuita (any meal works).
Not furui (things only) or ookii: 'older than me' is watashi yori toshi ga ue (toshiue), and younger is toshishita.

english: make yourself understood; speak the same language
trap: Not wakaru: being understood in a language is tsuujiru, usually with the language as the subject (eigo tsuujiru?, nihongo ga tsuujita).
Not akusesarii o kiru: earrings, necklaces and badges take tsukeru, or just suru (piasu shiteru).
Not kontakuto o kakeru like glasses: lenses go in with ireru and come out with hazusu or toru.
Not mafuraa o kiru: a scarf takes suru (mafuraa shiteru), or maku 'wrap' for the act of putting it on.
English 'put your hair up' doesn't carry over; the verb is musubu 'tie' (casually kami shibaru or matomeru).
Not shuuden o misu suru: Japanese says the last train 'is gone', as in shuuden nakunatchau!
Not nimotsu o oku or nimotsu o nokosu: handing bags over to be kept (hotel, locker, airport check-in) is azukeru. Leaving them behind by mistake is wasureru.
Not densha ga hanareru or densha ga saru: a train or bus leaving is just deru, as in tsugi no densha nanji ni deru?
Not uchi o hanareru or nokosu: leaving home for the day is deru, and the place you leave takes o.
English 'vacuum' is a verb, but Japanese says soujiki o kakeru, not soujiki suru or soujiki o tsukau.
Not kakeru or tsurusu: laundry put out to dry is hosu, and the noun is sentakumono (the clothes), not sentaku.
No English verb leads here: bed hair 'sticks on' (neguse ga tsuku), as in neguse tsuiteru yo.
Not sentakuki o hashiraseru or ugokasu: you 'spin' (mawasu) the washer.
Not gohan o ryouri suru or niru: rice has its own verb, taku.
There is no 'get' to translate: it is the verb you, and the drink takes ni (not o).
Not osake o takusan moteru: a heavy drinker is 'strong at alcohol'; with the drink as topic (kono osake wa tsuyoi) it means the drink is strong.
Not aji ga tsuyoi: heavy salt or sauce flavour is koi.
Not shouyu o oku or ireru: sauce poured over food is kakeru (also mayo, dressing, sauce).
The rice cooker finishing is gohan ga taketa; gohan ga dekita means the whole meal is ready.
Meat being cooked through is yakeru ('it got grilled'), not niku ga dekita.
A forecast doesn't machigaeru (that is a person's mistake) or chigau. It misses, hazureru, or hits, ataru.
English 'the weather turns/breaks' points to kawaru or kowareru. Worsening weather 'crumbles': kuzureru.
English has no verb for it: the rainy season is 'entered', tsuyu ni hairu, and when it ends it 'opens', tsuyu ga akeru.
English 'there's a rainbow' points to niji ga aru. A rainbow comes out: niji ga deru (or niji ga kakaru).
Not hakike ga aru: nausea 'does', hakike ga suru; in casual talk people say kimochi warui.
Guessable; only the tense trips people: tired eyes now is me ga tsukareta / tsukareteru.
The ankle isn't named: you sprain the ashi, ashi o kujiku (ashi kujiita), or nenza shita.
There is no 'turn up' verb: volume up is oto o ookiku suru ('make the sound big') and down is chiisaku suru; oto o ageru / sageru also work.
Not deru: 'it came out nice' is kirei ni toreta / yoku toreteru (it got taken well).
Not just insutooru suru: everyday 'get the app' is apuri o ireru ('put in'); deleting it is kesu.
Not okuru: okuru sends to a person; putting a photo up online is ageru ('raise') or appu suru, as in insuta ni ageta.
Not kowareru: a cracked screen wareru ('splits'); kowareru means the phone stopped working.
For a phone or online video the everyday word is douga; bideo suggests a camcorder or tape. The verb is the same toru as for photos.
waifai aru? is fine, but natives often ask waifai tonderu? ('is Wi-Fi flying?'), which is opaque if you only know tobu as 'fly'.
Not shukudai o morau: homework 'comes out', shukudai ga deta (we got homework). It is the intransitive half of shukudai o dasu.
'I got paid' is the pay 'coming in', kyuuryou haitta (or kyuuryou ga deta), not a passive of harau.
Not 'shiroi hito', which reads as 'a white person': fair skin is iro ga shiroi ('colour is white'). Iro ga kuroi means tanned.

english: lay out the futon (make up the bed)
trap: Not futon o tsukuru or futon o oku: you spread bedding out with shiku. Putting it away is futon o tatamu (fold) or shimau.
Nothing in English 'run a bath' points to wakasu: Japanese heats the bath, the same verb as oyu o wakasu. When it's ready: ofuro waita yo. Ofuro o ireru is also heard.
Not okane o kowasu or waru: breaking a note into change is kuzusu, 'crumble'. For example, ichiman en kuzushite moraemasu ka.
There's no adjective for 'picky': it's 'many likes and dislikes', sukikirai ga ooi (or ga hageshii). Not picky at all: sukikirai nai.
Not tamago o wakasu: wakasu is for boiling water. Cooking food in boiling water (eggs, pasta, noodles) is yuderu.
Not sumaho ga kooru: kooru is ice. A frozen screen 'hardens' with katamaru. Furiizu suru is also heard.

english: pollen is in the air (hay-fever season)
trap: English 'the pollen count is high' has nothing to translate. Japanese pollen 'flies' with tobu: kafun tonderu ne.

english: see a doctor, get checked by a doctor
trap: Not isha o miru, which means you look at the doctor. The doctor looks at you: isha ni mite morau.
Not wasuremono o oku: leaving something behind is wasuremono o suru, or just wasureta.
You don't need a word for 'handwriting': say ji ga kirei or ji ga kitanai (the characters are neat or messy).
Not sumaho o kowashita, unless you broke it: 'my phone broke' is intransitive, sumaho kowareta.
Not gohan ga junbi da: 'dinner's ready!' is gohan dekita yo (dekiru = come into being).
Not nikibi o morau: spots, rashes and blisters 'form', so nikibi dekichatta.
Dipping is tsukeru, pouring over is kakeru: sushi ni shouyu tsukeru, but toufu ni shouyu kakeru.
Not tsukeru or kiru: belts and ties are shimeru ('tighten'). Casually, shiitoberuto shite.
English 'get out' pushes toward deru. Families say ofuro agatta? ('came up out of the bath').
Not uchi ni hairu: you step up into a home, so 'come on in' is douzo agatte.

english: take, walk or drive someone home
trap: Not tsurete iku: seeing someone home is okuru ('send'), so okutte iku yo, or eki made okuru.
Not megusuri o ireru or nomu: eye drops take sasu, the same verb as kasa o sasu.
Not gohan o oku: leaving food on your plate is nokosu, as in nokoshite ii? or nokosanaide.
Not koe o nakusu: a hoarse voice 'withers', as in karaoke de koe kareta.
Not kiru or tsukeru: creams and lotions are spread on, so nuru (the paint verb).
Not atsui ga dame: 'I can't take heat (or cold)' is atsusa ni yowai / samusa ni yowai. It's the osake ga yowai idea with ni.
Not tsuyu ga owaru: the rainy season 'opens out' (akeru), the same akeru as yo ga akeru (day breaks).
English has a verb, but in Japanese a sneeze 'comes out' (kushami ga deru); kushami o suru also works.

english: get a cramp in one's leg
trap: Not ashi ni kuranpu ga aru: a cramping leg 'tsuru' (pulls tight). It's usually said in the past: ashi tsutta!
Not bansoukou o kiru or kakeru: anything stuck on flat (plasters, compresses, stickers, posters) is haru.

english: turn on the tap / the water
trap: Not mizu o tsukeru: tsukeru is for lights and power, while water is 'let out' (dasu).
Not sentakumono o ireru or motte kuru: laundry is 'taken in' (torikomu). Example: ame futte kita, sentakumono torikonde!
Switches are 'put in' (ireru) to turn on and 'cut' (kiru) to turn off, not tsukeru and kesu.
Not osake o ireru: ireru is for making tea and coffee, while pouring into someone's glass is tsugu.
Japanese has no verb for 'dump': you get 'shaken off' (furu, passive furareru), as in kanojo ni furareta. Don't confuse it with ame ni furareru.
Not just yoku kikoenai: the set phrase is 'the phone is far', as in chotto denwa ga tooi n desu ga.
English 'turn off' leads to kesu; a ringing alarm is stopped: tomeru.

english: get worn out, tiredness builds up
trap: English 'worn out' gives only tsukareta; built-up tiredness is a noun that tamaru (piles up), like sutoresu ga tamaru.
English 'yawn' is one verb; Japanese is a noun that deru (comes out), or akubi o suru.
Not shakkuri ga aru: hiccups deru, and 'I can't stop hiccupping' is shakkuri ga tomaranai.
Not kasa o shimeru: an umbrella is folded, tatamu; opening it is sasu (or hiraku).
